code.title: Java passes copies: primitive, mutate, reassign

followUps:
Pack them into one object: a small array, a record, or a tiny class. Java returns exactly one value, so you wrap several. Example: return new int[]{min, max}; or record MinMax(int min, int max) {} and return new MinMax(2, 9);.

Arrays only suit values of one type; a record gives names and types, so prefer it. Another option is passing a mutable holder in, but that hides the output and is harder to read.

Nothing the caller can see: the caller's String is unchanged. s += "x" builds a new String and points the local parameter at it, and the parameter is only a copy of the reference.

Example: caller has t = "hi", method does s += "x", so inside s is "hix" but t is still "hi". Strings are also immutable, so there is no way to change the original object. Use the return value (t = add(t)) or a StringBuilder, which is mutable.

C++ int& is a true alias of the caller's variable, so assigning to it changes the caller's variable. Java has no such thing; a Java parameter is always its own copy.

In C++ void inc(int& x){ x++; } turns a caller's 5 into 6. In Java void inc(int x){ x++; } leaves the caller at 5. Likewise a C++ swap with references works, while a Java swap of two parameters cannot.

code.title: while versus do-while on the input 0

followUps:
It is an infinite loop with no init, no condition and no update. A missing condition means true, so it repeats forever until a break, return or exception leaves it.

It is equivalent to while (true). Example: for (;;) { if (read() == -1) break; } keeps reading until the end marker. Without an exit the program never finishes, so always make sure one path can leave the loop.

Because for-each uses an iterator, and the list notices if it was structurally changed (add or remove) behind the iterator's back. The iterator then throws on its next step instead of giving wrong results.

Example: list [1,2,3], and inside for (int x : list) you call list.remove(...); the next iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException. The list keeps a modification counter and the iterator compares it. Fix it with iterator.remove() or list.removeIf(...).

code.title: Fall-through versus arrow switch

followUps:
No, one switch must use one style. Mixing case 1: and case 2 -> in the same switch is a compile error.

Pick colon form (with fall-through and break) or arrow form (no fall-through). You can have a colon-style switch in one place and an arrow-style switch in another, just not both inside the same braces. Arrow form is usually safer, so prefer it on Java 14 and later.

yield hands back the result of a block branch in a switch expression, much like return does for a method.

Example: int n = switch (s) { case "a" -> 1; default -> { int t = s.length(); yield t * 2; } };. A single-expression arrow branch gives its value directly; only a braced block needs yield. It also works in colon-style switch expressions (case 1: yield 5;).

code.title: Switch expression and pattern matching (Java 21)

followUps:
Because then the compiler checks that you handled every constant. If someone adds a new enum value later, the switch expression stops compiling and shows you the places to fix.

With default, the new constant would silently fall into it and may do the wrong thing. Example: enum Color {RED, GREEN} gets BLUE added; a switch expression over RED and GREEN without default fails to compile until you add BLUE. (Java inserts a runtime error for separately compiled code.)

It throws NullPointerException, even if there is a default label. Only Java 21 pattern switches can accept null, through an explicit case null.

The classic String switch calls s.hashCode() first, and calling a method on null fails. Guard with if (s == null) before switching, or in Java 21 write case null -> ... yourself.

code.title: String switch: hashing and the null NullPointerException

followUps:
Both are bytecode jump tables chosen by the compiler. tableswitch is used when the case values are dense (like 1,2,3,4), and indexes straight into a table in O(1). lookupswitch is used for sparse values (like 1, 100, 5000) and searches sorted key/target pairs, usually with binary search in O(log n).

You do not choose; the compiler picks whichever is smaller or faster. Either way, the source code is the same.

Yes, if it is a final variable initialised with a constant expression, because it is then a compile-time constant. A normal non-final local, or a final one set from a method call, is not allowed.

Example: final int LIMIT = 10; switch (x) { case LIMIT: ... } compiles; final int v = read(); then case v: does not. Case labels must also be unique, so two constants of the same value fail.

code.title: Labelled break and continue in a grid

followUps:
In a while loop, continue jumps straight to the condition check. In a for loop it jumps to the update step (like i++) and then the condition.

This is why a continue in a while loop whose increment sits at the bottom can loop forever: while (i < 5) { if (i == 2) continue; i++; } never moves past 2. In a for loop for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) the update still runs, so it is safe.

No, a plain break or continue cannot jump out of a switch expression. The compiler rejects it, since an expression must produce a value. Use yield for the value, or throw an exception.

A classic switch statement allows break, and the arrow-style statement does too. If you need to leave an enclosing loop from inside a switch statement, use a labelled break such as break outer; or restructure into a method with return.

code.title: Overloading picks by static type, overriding by real object

followUps:
Static methods can be overloaded, but not overridden. A subclass static method with the same signature only hides the parent's; the choice is made from the declared type, not the real object.

Example: Animal a = new Dog(); with static Animal.hello() and Dog.hello(): a.hello() runs Animal's version. Instance methods would run Dog's. Overloads like static int add(int,int) and static double add(double,double) are fine.

It calls print(Object), because overloads are picked at compile time from the declared type, and o is declared as Object even though it holds a String.

Only print(Object) is applicable for that static type, so the String version is never considered. To reach the String overload cast: print((String) o). Overriding is different: that is decided at run time by the real object.

code.title: Overload resolution phases: widening beats boxing

followUps:
Because Java allows only one conversion step at a time in the strict and loose phases: widening then boxing is not a recognised pair. A byte can widen to long or box to Byte, but not become a Long.

Example: void f(Long x) called as f((byte) 5) fails to compile. Boxing yields Byte, and Byte is not a Long. By contrast boxing then widening (int to Integer to Object) is allowed. Fix with f(5L).

Pass an Integer object: list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) or list.remove((Integer) 1). A plain remove(1) means index 1.

Example with [10, 1, 5]: remove(1) deletes the element at index 1 (the value 1), giving [10, 5], while remove(Integer.valueOf(10)) deletes the value 10, giving [1, 5]. The primitive int exact match wins in the first phase, before boxing is tried.

code.title: Varargs: array inside, empty call, asList trap

followUps:
Because format needs to accept any number of arguments of any type, and every type is an Object. Primitives get boxed automatically into the Object array.

Example: String.format("%s is %d", "Ann", 30) builds new Object[]{"Ann", 30}. That is flexible but allocates an array and boxes each number on every call, which is why hot paths avoid it.

It promises that the method only reads from the varargs array and does not store it or let it escape. The compiler then drops the unchecked "heap pollution" warning for generic varargs.

Example: @SafeVarargs static <T> List<T> of(T... xs) that copies the elements is safe. If it returned the array as Object[] or assigned a wrong type into it, a later ClassCastException could appear far from the cause. It is allowed only on static, final or private methods and constructors.

code.title: Jagged arrays, shallow clone and deepToString

followUps:
Copy every row, not just the outer array. A loop does it: for (i...) copy[i] = grid[i].clone();. Calling grid.clone() only copies the row references, so both grids share the same rows.

Short version: int[][] copy = Arrays.stream(grid).map(int[]::clone).toArray(int[][]::new);. Cost is O(rows * cols) time and the same extra space. Check: after a deep copy, setting copy[0][0] = 9 leaves grid[0][0] unchanged.

Arrays.toString(grid) prints row objects as unhelpful addresses like [[I@1b6d3586, ...]; Arrays.deepToString(grid) prints the real contents like [[1, 2], [3, 4]].

toString is shallow, so it calls toString on each row, which is just the default Object text. deepToString walks nested arrays recursively. Use it for debug printing of 2D arrays; for loops or streams give custom layouts.

code.title: Array covariance, boxing and conversions

followUps:
About 4 to 5 times more for the object array in the common case. int[1000] is about 4 KB of numbers (plus a small header). Integer[1000] holds 1000 references (4 to 8 bytes each) plus up to 1000 Integer objects of about 16 bytes each.

Roughly 4 KB versus 20 to 24 KB, and the Integer data is scattered in memory, so scans are slower. Small values from -128 to 127 are cached and shared, which saves objects there but not the references.

Use streams: list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray() for List to int[], and Arrays.stream(a).boxed().toList() for int[] to List. A plain Arrays.asList(intArray) does not work: it gives a List of one int[].

Example: [3, 1, 2] as int[] becomes a List with elements 3, 1, 2 after boxed(). Each direction copies n elements, so it costs O(n) time and space, and boxing allocates objects for values outside the small cache.

code.title: asList view, List.of immutable, ArrayList copy

followUps:
Because List.of does not allow null elements at all, it rejects them immediately with a NullPointerException. This is a design choice: nulls in collections cause surprise failures later.

The immutable collections (List.of, Set.of, Map.of) all reject null, and Set.of also rejects duplicates. If you truly need nulls use Arrays.asList(1, null) or an ArrayList. Many people consider "no nulls" a feature, since contains(null) on List.of also throws.

It gives a read-only view of another list, but it does not make the data immutable. Whoever holds the original list can still change it, and the view shows those changes.

Example: List<Integer> v = Collections.unmodifiableList(orig); orig.add(4); now v has the 4 too, while v.add(5) throws UnsupportedOperationException. For a real snapshot use List.copyOf(orig), which copies the elements into an immutable list.

code.title: Stable sort and the subtraction comparator bug

followUps:
Pass a reversed comparator and use an Integer[]: Arrays.sort(a, Collections.reverseOrder());. Comparators do not work on primitive int[].

For an int[], either sort ascending then reverse in place (swap a[i] with a[n-1-i]) or use Arrays.stream(a).boxed().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray(). Example: [3,1,2] sorts to [1,2,3] and reverses to [3,2,1]. Cost O(n log n) time.

Because subtraction can overflow and flip the sign, so the sort order becomes wrong or inconsistent. Use Integer.compare(a, b) instead.

Example: a = 2,000,000,000 and b = -2,000,000,000. The true difference 4,000,000,000 does not fit in an int, so a - b wraps to a negative number, claiming a is smaller. TimSort may then also throw "Comparison method violates its general contract".

code.title: Strings are immutable: result must be assigned

followUps:
Because split takes a regular expression, and an unescaped dot means "any character". Every character is a separator, so all the pieces are empty strings and trailing empties are dropped, leaving a length-0 array.

Escape it: "a.b".split("\\.") gives [a, b], and Pattern.quote(".") also works. Same trap for |, *, +, $ and ?.

It returns 2, because length() counts UTF-16 chars, not what you see as one symbol. The emoji needs two chars (a surrogate pair).

Use s.codePointCount(0, s.length()) to get 1. Likewise charAt may return half of a symbol. For loops over real characters use s.codePoints(). This only matters for characters beyond the basic range, such as emoji and some rare scripts.

code.title: equals, ==, compareTo and case-insensitive sorting

followUps:
Because toLowerCase() uses the machine's default locale, and in Turkish uppercase I becomes dotless lowercase i, not the plain i. Comparisons like "TITLE".toLowerCase().equals("title") then fail on that machine.

Pass an explicit locale for technical text: s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT), or use equalsIgnoreCase. Use the user's locale only when showing text to a person.

Use the built-in comparator: Arrays.sort(words, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); or list.sort(String::compareToIgnoreCase).

Example: [b, A, c] sorts plainly to [A, b, c] because uppercase letters have smaller codes, but [apple, Banana] stays wrong-looking as [Banana, apple] without it; with it you get [apple, Banana]. For language-aware ordering with accents use Collator.getInstance(locale). Cost is O(n log n) comparisons.
